_comment: Failures the first-run harness may report and STILL exit 0 -- each with a written reason.
WHY AN ALLOWLIST RATHER THAN DELETING THE CHECK. A deleted check takes its reasoning with it:
next year nobody can tell whether the case was considered and accepted, or never thought of.
This file makes acceptance a visible, reviewable claim -- the same shape as
corpus-parse-allowlist.json and dsl-coverage-allowlist.json elsewhere in this repo.
- An entry is an admission, not a fix. Keep the list short and re-read it when it grows.
- The harness still PRINTS every accepted failure, loudly, on every run. Accepted is not
- A failure NOT in this list still turns the run red. That is the whole point: the exit code
- `id` matches the check label the harness prints, exactly.

why: `npdev doctor` exits non-zero on a fresh clone because the runtimehost jars are not staged
yet -- which is TRUE, and is exactly what the next documented command (`./npdev setup`)
fixes. The command is a diagnostic: reporting an unmet precondition IS its job, and it
names the remedy in the same breath.
The alternatives were both worse. Reordering README to run `setup` before `doctor` would
make a user with the wrong Java spend ~10 minutes building jars before being told. Making
`runtimehost-jars` a WARN would change the meaning of a check id that is frozen by
manager/helpers/checks-contract.json and that the Manager's Ready screen renders.
So the harness's own rule -- every documented command must exit 0 -- is the thing that is
too strong here, for a documented check-then-fix sequence. Accepted rather than silently
special-cased in the script, so the judgement is reviewable.
accepted.revisitWhen: doctor stops reporting unstaged jars as a failure, or README stops documenting `doctor` before `setup`.
